speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to be able to participate in this debate.
I would like to begin my remarks by saying that I, along with other members in this Chamber, condemn Iraq for its invasion of Kuwait. In fact, not only Iraq, but its president should be condemned for many other actions it has taken in recent years. Saddam Hussein should not be the leader of that country. In fact, should be locked away.
I would like to pay tribute to the troops who are now in that area of the world, to the embassy staff in that region under a very difficult situation and also to the Canadian citizens in that region. Of course, my thoughts go out to those people and members of their families in Canada who are very concerned about their welfare, and particularly to one individual in the City of Moose Jaw, Paul Francoeur, a member of the armed forces presently in the Middle East. My best wishes and thoughts go out to him and his family.
I would like to take a slightly different approach than some members have been taking with respect to this debate and focus on a couple of areas; the role and purpose of the United Nations, and with respect to democracy here in this country.
The existence of the United Nations fundamentally, is to provide peace and harmony in this world. Since it was created at the end of World War II, it has suffered many setbacks and has struggled during its history. I believe that the recent actions and resolutions passed by the United Nations have had the most unified support that the UN has perhaps ever experienced.
One of the reasons for that support has been the turn-around by the Americans. These days the United States is praising the United Nations.
This has not always been the case. It was not very long ago that the United States was calling for the United Nations to leave New York. The United States still owes some $750 million to the United Nations and, perhaps, should be considering paying its contribution.

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
I would suggest that the United States is not so much concerned with the United Nations as it is concerned with a steady and secure oil supply. I am also concerned about its military intentions in that area of the world. Certainly an Iraq that controls a Kuwait controls a significant amount of the world's oil production and could have a significant impact on the United States.
The desire for extended military bases in that area certainly is part of the Americans' decision to take the action that they have. I am very glad that the United States has taken the position that it has in respect of Iraq in condemning it. However, I would question some of its motives.
If the UN is now so important, why does not the United States support resolution 242 which calls for Israel to withdraw from occupied territories that it has occupied since 1967? It is interesting that since the United States has been moving into that area of the world it has now found new criticism recently for Israel because it is looking for support for the Arab nations.
President Bush said that we could not have a dictatorship running a country in this world and imposing its will on people throughout its territory. We have noticed in the past that the United States condoned Panama, for example. Panama had a dictator for years, and it was involved in the drug trade. In fact there were implications connecting General Noriega to the CIA itself. Only when General Noriega's plans did not fit with the United States did it invade Panama.
This is a similar line to that which the United States took in places like Grenada and in its attacks on Libya. Why did not the United States condemn Dictator Hussein when he invaded Iran back in 1980? There was no action when Iraq chemically gassed the Kurds, resulting in some 4,000 terrible deaths in 1988 that inflicted a lot of pain and suffering on a lot of individuals and causing thousands of injuries which people will suffer from for the rest of their lives. Also there was no condemnation of Syrian and Israeli occupation of Lebanon. What about the occupation of East Timor by Indonesia?
I am very glad that the United States has taken a turn for the best with respect to the United Nations and has condemned the actions of Iraq, but it is certainly with questionable intention that the United States has taken this action. When the United States announced that it
would be sending troops into that area of the world, it did so long before UN resolution 665 and without prior consultation. It was only when UN policy happened to coincide with U.S. policy that the U.S. began to sing the United Nations praises.
In respect of all of that we have our Government in Canada supporting a U.S. position long before the UN resolution. I would suggest that the Prime Minister acted in a fashion that has affected and harmed the reputation of this country in the world.
Why would the Prime Minister and why would this country take the actions it did in light of the background I just highlighted in respect of the United States? This decision seems to have been made on the spur of the moment. On August 3, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs had indicated that he no intention of any military action in the Middle East. On August 6, the Prime Minister met with President Bush. On August 10, after a NATO meeting, the Prime Minister announced that Canada would be sending two naval destroyers and a supply ship into the Middle East. This was a very quick turnaround. In fact the announcement by Canada was made two weeks before the UN passed Resolution 665. That resolution, of course, is the one which authorized UN member states to take necessary measures against shipping to ensure strict implementation of the UN sanctions.
With respect to the government, I think that has hurt Canada's reputation in the world. It has hurt our reputation as a peacekeeping nation. It is the first time since the Second World War, I believe, that we have sent Canadian ships under a Canadian flag into a potential war zone. I think that action by the Prime Minister was one that certainly should have led him to call Parliament back immediately. He did not. In fact, Parliament was not called back until its scheduled date of September 24. At that time this debate began, Mr. Speaker.
This action is not justifiable. The government considered it to be important, but when you consider it in light of other actions, one wonders about the respect that this government has for democracy in this country. In August 1987, when 174 refugees landed on the coast of Nova Scotia, the government considered that an emergency situation and immediately called back the House of Commons to sit. Yet, when the Prime Minister announced that for the first time since the Second World War we are going to be sending Canadian ships into a
October 18, 1990

potential war zone under a Canadian flag, he did not call back the House.
Other governments called back their parliaments. They certainly did in Britain. The absence of such action shows this government's lack of respect for democracy.
This has to be taken in the context of the attitude that Canadians have today toward parliamentarians right across this country. People are questioning parliamentarians and their actions, certainly the actions in the Senate with the banging of chairs and the blowing of kazoos.
This government's use of time allocation and closure, time after time after time, have made people become disillusioned with this institution of Parliament. We have a motion that the government wants to limit committee size because it feels that committees in this House on occasion are disagreeing with the government. It is an infringement of an MPs right to properly perform his duty. This is simply one more example of that. It is one more example of this government failing to respect the democratic institutions of this country and causing this institution to be held in less regard by the people in this nation.
What is required in this situation? We must make the role of the United Nations in the world a priority. As such, Canada should be taking a leading role as a member of the Security Council to ensure, first of all, that the UN takes charge of military operations over in the Middle East. As well, we should declare that our ships will only go as far as originally planned, and that is to the Gulf of Oman, and strictly for the purpose of helping to enforce the UN sanctions against Iraq under Resolution 665. That and no more, Mr. Speaker.
As well, Canada should be focusing more attention on the problem of the refugee situation. Thousands of refugees from numerous nations have been fleeing Kuwait and that region of the world. As is often the case with refugees, they become almost invisible. People tend to forget about them. They get quick exposure on the media and then they are forgotten. Although the government has committed some funds, which is very laudable, there should be a stronger commitment than that. Canada should be committing itself to spending more
Government Orders
attention and energy with respect to the refugee problem.
In conclusion, I would simply like to say that I was very disappointed in the actions which the government had taken. It certainly had a bad reflection on the United Nations. It has also had a very bad reflection on the way Canadians view this Parliament. It has shown a disregard for democracy in this country.
With those remarks, I would close by saying that I will certainly be supporting my party's amendment and opposing the government's resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief.
I congratulate the hon. member on an excellent speech. I just want to take this opportunity to ask the hon. member, who is well known not only in Saskatchewan but throughout this country as a tireless defender of farmers, if he could elaborate on the implications of this serious crisis for grain farmers in particular.
What impact will this have on western farmers? I know that Canadians will await with interest the comments and the assistance of the hon. member on this important question.

Mr. Speaker, we have in this country today an rural infrastructure that is in real danger. It has been shrinking for a number of years and now it is simply beginning to collapse.
One of the reasons it is collapsing is the economic base, whether it be fishing in Nova Scotia, growing apples in the Annapolis Valley, or growing grain in western Canada. This government has failed to address the agricultural issue properly in the last number of years. Certainly since it has taken power it has been promising to bring in an agricultural program since 1985.
With respect to this situation, Iraq was our fourth largest customer with respect to grain. It is certainly an important customer. The loss of Iraq is simply adding to the difficulties that exist today. We have in Canada a problem with grain sales. One of the main reasons is that we have the United States which, through its Export Enhancement Program, is infringing on our traditional territory certainly in the U.S.S.R. and in Africa. We are

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
having difficulties making sales into those areas and then we lose Iraq. It has a devastating effect. That is why we now have literally thousands of bushels sitting in fields.
It is important for this government when it brings in its agricultural program that there be compensation made with respect to the loss of those sales. It is not the farmers' fault in western Canada that Iraq invaded Kuwait. It is not the farmers' fault that this government is not taking action against the United States for infringing on our traditional sales areas and markets. It is not the farmers' fault and the farmers should not be suffering.
This government should be taking some action, which it has not so far, to rectify that situation and assist farmers and, in doing so, will assist all of rural Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise and say a few words on this motion before the House with respect to the Iraqi situation. It is particularly appropriate as we come up to November 11 and Remembrance Day.
I have been approached by a vast majority of my constituents who are in agreement with the actions of our government and the United Nations acting together. I met with many people from particularly eastern Europe. They have told me in no uncertain terms that we all know the history during the thirties when there were four or five times that Mr. Hitler could have been stopped. At that time other countries were faced with a choice. They could have stopped him or they could not. They lacked the courage or the moral fortitude to stand up and block him the four or five times when they could have. As a result, we got into a world war where 40 million people, at a minimum estimate, lost their lives. How many more tens of millions were injured, wounded, or physically or mentally affected is unknown.
Europe was destroyed as an infrastructure, whether it was roads or buildings or schools, and only recently are they beginning to recover and thrive. More than 40,000 Canadians died. That has had an impact on families and family trees. I know my own family tree in Britain was totally finished. The last Thacker in Britain in our family
tree was lost in Sicily. That has had quite an impact on everybody. You do not forget those things.
It is ironic that just at the time when eastern Europe was coming on side and adopting more approaches that were conciliatory, the United Nations was expanding, the GATT treaty was expanding and human rights were expanding, time when it seemed that we could move on to a new world order with peace and a much more co-operative relationship, we would be faced with Saddam Hussein. He is an individual like Hitler was when he took over a country, who has absolutely no conception of human rights or the feelings of other people. He simply invaded Kuwait, which everyone agrees was a total illegal act by any and all standards.
The bottom line is that our generation is faced with the same choice as our ancestors of two generations ago. We can either stop it now or we can appease or somehow rationalize it in our own minds as none of our affair.
The United Nations has decided that it is our affair and acting together is a good precedent. I hope we will continue to act together and give the Security Council the backing and the support that it needs. That is our hope. We do not have any other models, we have to use the United Nations. It is a wonderful model and the clauses are there. We have to be prepared to act together and I think we will. The fact is that we simply do not have any choice.
Even with conventional weapons we have no choice. We simply cannot afford a world war with conventional weapons. We all know we certainly cannot afford one with nuclear weapons.
I am proud to say, and I am sure I speak for the vast majority of my constituents, that Canada is part of this. Thanks should go to our navy, the men and women on those ships, in the air force and their support staff. We are thinking of them. They have our full support. We worry about them and we want them to come home without any shots being fired and certainly no one being injured or killed. They have our support.

I have a short comment, Mr. Speaker. I will be participating in the debate tonight.
I want my colleague to understand that in no way, shape or form do I intend to defend the actions of
October 18, 1990

Saddam Hussein. I see the hon. member repeating the line well used by the President of the United States, Mr. Bush, comparing Saddam Hussein with Hitler. I do not know why.
Could the hon. member enlighten us as to when the western world suddenly discovered that Saddam Hussein, who for eight years has become quite well known for his tactics, and well armed by the west I might add, fit the description of Hitler. Is it now or was it recently or was it when he was doing what we could not do against Iran?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that my colleague opposite and friend for many years raises a good point. The point is when do nations act? Leaders and dictators all over the world get away with all sorts of atrocities within their own country and the world does not act. There have been all sorts of instances of Saddam Hussein killing his own people. We are a world that is divided into nation states and we accept that concept of nation states. They have all sorts of rights within their own nations to do things that we do not agree with, against human rights and otherwise, and we do not act against them. But when Saddam Hussein moved into Kuwait, that jelled everyone's thinking that this man was a madman. This man is a madman. This man knows no constraints, none of the ordinary constraints that leaders in practically every other country in the world now are beginning to accept and to operate within. Therefore, it did become a threat.
I know the arguments that it is because of oil and all of that, and there is no doubt that is a major fact because without oil imports, even in this country, we would be in very deep trouble. The United States is in even deeper trouble as well as other countries of the world. I do not take away one moment if he says we acted only for oil.
I think there was an imperative that went beyond just oil. So many other nations, including the Arab nations themselves, have joined together to say, "Okay, he has got to be stopped now". I think there was a time, if my friend wanted us to do it 10 years ago, well I would not take that away from him. He may well be right, but certainly now we have enough people standing together that I think that in and of itself that is good enough to stop Saddam Hussein. Hopefully it will be an example to
Government Orders
other dictators who will act without any sense of consideration for other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. I declare at the outset I support unequivocally the part of the motion which states:
That this House condemn the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq -
I cannot however support the concluding part of the motion which states:
- take part in the multinational military effort in and around the
Arabian Peninsula -
Why, you may ask, Mr. Speaker. I begin my answers by asking two questions. Is Canada prepared to support military action against Iraq outside of the United Nations auspices? Is Canada prepared to support military action against Iraq without full debate in Parliament and full consultation with the opposition? The latter part of the government's motion, as it now stands, could be a blank cheque and for that reason I oppose the government's motion.
Let me proceed, Mr. Speaker, by remembering a past Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, a man who strongly endorsed the use of international diplomacy as means to settle international conflict. However, we saw a change in 1984 when the Conservatives under Brian Mulroney came to power. We witnessed a changed in attitude from a Canadian policy based solely now using Mr. Mulroney's own words, "super relations with the United States".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would hope that the hon. member would address him as the Prime Minister when referring to the right hon. gentlemen. You are addressing him as the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, it should be the Prime Minister.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your reminder.
This subservient attitude towards President George Bush's foreign policy was evident in many of Canada's past actions that relate to the United States interests. It was there when the United States invaded Panama against Noriega; it was there again when President Bush led the American military into the Persian gulf. It was there once more when Canada's response came more than two weeks before the United Nations agreed to endorse the use of military force to ensure compliance to sanctions. While Mr. Mulroney argued that it was part of

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
a multinational effort, it was clearly initially a United States effort.
Let us not forget that the resolution passed by the United Nations endorses the use of military force to back up the economic embargo of Iraq. There is no mandate to use force to invade that country. There is no mandate to use force to invade that country.
I do not question the Prime Minister's statement of September 24, in this House, and I quote:
Our contribution to the defence of freedom and our resistance of
aggression constitute chapters of sacrifice and glory in the history of
this nation.
But I question Canada's initial involvement in this crisis as sanctioned by this government, in the absence of clear, United Nations is stewardship with Parliamentary debate in this House. I cannot trust this government with a blank cheque on this issue.
I will support the government's resolution provided we receive certain assurances from this government regarding the future or deployment of Canadian forces and the involvement of Canada in a Gulf war; specifically, a commitment that no changes in Canada's position will take place until Parliament or the opposition has been consulted and secondly, that Canada does not participate in offensive military action outside United Nations auspices without the approval of Parliament.
It should be made clear that our party took the the initiative for an all-party agreement on the resolution, not this government and definitely not the New Democratic Party.
I should point out that the approach to Canadian foreign policy by this government during the last six years has sharply turned from a strong Canadian voice to either sitting on the sidelines, or to cheering the policy initiatives of the United States with little or no consultation with our Parliament.
At this juncture I ask this government: Where was the Prime Minister during the crisis? In Washington. Who advised the Prime Minister at this time? President Bush. What were the United Nations members doing when the Prime Minister was in Washington? They were recalling their parliaments to debate the crisis with their citizens. Did we do it in Canada? Sadly, Mr. Speaker, we did not.
Sending troops to the Gulf is a national emergency, and sending troops into a possible war zone is not a decision that the Prime Minister should make on his own. The issue should be brought before Parliament for all to debate. Debate is essential in a democracy or democracy withers and dies.
I now ask if this government is prepared to make a commitment that there will not be a further deployment of troops, or the use of force without a clear mandate from our Parliament and under the stewardship of the United Nations.
What initiatives is this government making with the United Nations to find a peaceful resolution to this crisis?
In closing, I would like to say that Canadians are encouraged by the role that the United Nations has played in this crisis and we must seize this opportunity to assert the supremacy of that great institution and not of the United States. Let this be the objective that guides Canadian foreign policy.
Canada must continue to search for peace, just as Canada shall continue to abhor war. Is Canada prepared to support military action against Iraq, outside of United Nations auspices? Is Canada prepared to support military action against Iraq without full Parliamentary debate and consultation? Canada shall insist on acting militarily only under the United Nations umbrella, guided by the wisdom of this House. Hence, I support the amendment proposed by my party.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway.

I know that the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception is consulting with the hon. member in terms of a response to this question, but the member from Manitoba is his own member and hopefully will give his own answer.
The member knows that there have been discussions and dialogues in the House about some other form of a motion. The New Democratic Party has proposed a subamendment which I believe the hon. member has indicated he supports. His party has also proposed an amendment. Of course, the thrust of those amendments is to ensure that any action in the gulf must only be
October 18, 1990

under United Nations auspices. In the event that those amendments are defeated, does the hon. member intend to vote for or against the government motion?
Or, Mr. Speaker, is he going to stand up and say: "Well, you know, we are trying hard to get an agreement. We are working really hard. We are hoping that there can be an all-party resolution." Is he going to be direct? Is he going to be straightforward? Is he going to tell the House whether he supports the resolution or not?

Mr. Speaker, I have always been direct in the House and I thank the hon. member for recognizing that fact.
The hon. member was trying to insinuate that I was consulting with my hon. colleague. Of course, I would like to consult with my colleague. In this particular instance, there was no consultation.
To answer the question, the hon. member was not listening very clearly to all the provisions that I indicated. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Comments are now terminated. On debate, the hon. member for Davenport.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago in the House an alternative motion was put forward at page 14250 of Hansard which contains three principles. One principle is that Canada is against invasions of all kinds. The second is that Canada supports the United Nations and its resolutions since the Kuwait invasion. And the third is that there will be a debate in Parliament should there be an outbreak of hostilities involving Canadian forces.
That resolution, it seems to me, is highly commendable. It contains a lot of wisdom. It is the result of negotiations that my party has initiated with the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It has all the elements that would generate, I believe, a unanimous vote on the part of Parliament, which is extremely important if it is to have any impact at home and abroad.
We are against any form of invasion. In recent years, we have seen what happened in Afghanistan. You, Mr. Government Orders
Speaker, and many present here tonight will remember the outrage in public opinion throughout the world against that invasion.
We also recall, perhaps a little further in the past, the invasion of Tibet which, unfortunately, did not provoke much of an outrage in the world community. Not only that that, but it did not even provoke any movement of troops on the part of any of the superpowers to defend, protect, and restore the integrity of Tibet. I suspect that was due to the fact that Tibet does not have any oil wells. A comparison between the reaction of the world community to the invasion of Tibet and to the invasion of Kuwait is a very solitary and interesting lesson.
We have, in case of an outbreak of war in the Middle East, some horrendous consequences to contemplate, both in terms of human life and environmental damage. The debate here tonight does not lend itself to that kind of examination. I just want to make a very brief reference to that aspect which would horrify every thinking human being on this planet.
What disturbs us very much is that, in case of an outbreak, the line of command in that part of the world is not clearly defined. We do not know under whose command our troops and ships would be when the going gets rough. This is why we feel it is extremely desirable to find a way on Tuesday, when we vote on the motion, to adopt the proposed alternative put on the table only a couple of days ago. In that motion we have the establishment of a clear and important principle that it is under the flag of the UN and under the leadership of the world community as represented by the Security Council that our troops will operate.
We are in full agreement with the resolutions of the United Nations. We are in full agreement with the modus operandi of the United Nations. We believe there is a family of nations that function in this world, that it is a civilized one and basically very enlightened, and any territorial ambition or dispute, even the most legitimate perhaps within the boundaries of certain nations and public opinion of any given nation cannot be resolved by means of violence and invasion. This is the lesson of history which we have gradually, slowly, and painfully learned throughout time. Now, perhaps for the first time in a long time, the world community has coalesced behind this very important and critical point.

While we fully understand the importance of the presence of troops moved into the Middle East, we know that that has taken place in order to buy time. We know the solution can only be a political solution. It cannot be a military solution if it is to be a lasting one. That point was extremely well made, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will remember a few weeks ago, at the meeting that took place between Mr. Bush and Mr. Gorbachev. There were evidently the elements in that meeting for the search of a political solution. The means probably were different. The way of thinking in Washington is suddenly quite different than the way of thinking in Moscow as to how to get there is quite different, but I am convinced as I stand in the House, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you are too, that in both capitols the desire is to arrive at a political solution. The same applies in our House of Parliament. We want to arrive at a political solution, one that will bring us together rather than divide us when we vote on the motion on Tuesday.
For this reason, I appreciate very much the opportunity to participate in the debate, to reaffirm the confidence of my colleagues and myself in the final role of the United Nations, and to recall that it was under the leadership of a former Prime Minister of Canada before he became Prime Minister, namely Mr. Pearson, that Canada became an active initiator of peacekeeping missions in many parts of the world, some less publicized than others. I am glad to see that a Pearsonian sense of world responsibility by way of peacekeeping has also been continued and adopted by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs. Along that path, the government will have the full support of Canadians because deep down in the heart of every Canadian there is this confidence, this tremendous belief, that only through the United Nations can the diffusion of world disputes, differences, and potential dangers be achieved.

Mr. Speaker, as I begin my speech, I would like to remark that our colleague from Davenport gave an excellent analysis of the situation and the role of Canada in peacekeeping.
For those who were riveted to the radio and television in the past months after Iraq invaded Kuwait, many people were upset and with good reason. We were hoping for, and we got, quick response from the United Nations. The United States took immediate action, and Canada, contrary to its tradition of following the banner
of the United Nations, decided to deploy men and material to the Middle East crisis. But I guess it would be impossible to expect the average Canadian to really understand the whole complex situation that has been that of the Middle East ever since 1948, or hundreds of years, for that matter. It has always been a very complex problem and there are probably too many factors that come into play. Do not forget the Middle East, for all practical purposes, was the cradle of civilization as we know it. Yet the problems over the years have compounded themselves to the point that it is hard to distinguish what is fact and what is fiction, and where is the truth and where are the lies. God knows there is a lot of truth and there have been a lot of lies that have come out of the Middle East.
I guess many people have taken a position on this whole issue without knowing the facts, and I can understand. Members of Parliament, our fellow Canadians, and many people throughout the world maybe just do not have time or the inclination, or they do not want to take the time, to realize there are reasons why this kind of conflict that has developed in the Middle East. A tremendous amount of resentment has been built up throughout the years, and it is understandable. I would like to point out one particular paragraph that I thought summed it up quite well.
The Arab masses resent the role that the United States is now playing in the Gulf and the financial support that some Arab states are providing, all of which they perceive as designed to protect undemocratic and feudalistic governments. They can be expected to ask with frustration and anger how many houses, schools, hospitals and highways could these funds have built in poor Arab parts of the world? How many farms and factories could have been established for hungry Arabs?
Why should this enormous amount of Arab money be diverted for the perpetuation of unjust and outdated governments? It is the anger and the frustration which breeds the Saddam Hussein and the Ayatollah Khomeinis of the Middle East.
Mr. Speaker, it does not take a genius to understand that in the past years in the Middle East the Arab nations have constantly been frustrated, especially by the United States, in finding a solution in the Middle East,
October 18, 1990

especially for the Palestinians who were driven out of their own homes. Has there been any effort in the last 40 years by the great powers to recognize that people who were on this land for thousands of years were literally pushed aside? Today a lot of people and nations have the nerve to point to Palestinians and call them terrorists, in their own land. When is the truth going to be known that the Palestinians have been the victims, and what other homeland, the homeland of my father from Lebanon. He is a Semitic.
Where was the United States, where were the powerful nations of this country, when they let Lebanon be sacrificed? They sacrificed Lebanon to make it a battleground between the Syrians and the Israelis and anybody else who were peddling arms.
How much hypocrisy will there be and how many lies are they going to tell us before the truth will be known? It will be too late.
How many Palestinians have died? How many have lived in the desert? How many Lebanese? There is not a week that I do not have people of Lebanese background who write and call to me, trying to bring a sister, a sister-in-law, a brother, or an uncle. It has been frustrating for all those who understand that there has been a lack of justice.
We see the United States send over unbelievable amounts of military arms and men-to protect what, Mr. Speaker? God knows that I have often said that the Lebanese problem would have been solved if they had oil underneath their soil. But, no, they are there to protect a vested interest. The cost, in human lives, never bothered them. Traditionally, under the former Prime Minister of this country, we always followed the lead of the United Nations in world conflicts. We had developed a reputation. And even as fellow travellers to different parts of the world, we were looked up to with a great amount of respect and esteem. They had faith in us. I am afraid that this faith could be eroded when we have this kind of activity.
As I mentioned at the beginning, had there just been an attempt in years past to solve the problems of Lebanon which has been bleeding for the last 15 years. How much bleeding can it take? Those who speak up in the name of the suffering Lebanese, they overtook the
Government Orders
hometown of my father. The Israelis have it under occupation.
What about the Palestinians who have been the victims? They throw stones and they get bullets in return. Yet they are called terrorists in their own land. When is the truth going to be known? Does it make me anti-Zionist because I want the Lebanese people to live in peace and the Palestinians to have a piece of land that they can call their own?
It makes me think of a former journalist, James M. Mynafee, who is now deceased. Mr. Speaker, you probably remember that name from the past. He wrote a book. I always liked the title. He asked at the time what Canada's role was. Was Canada a peacemaker or a powder-monkey? In the late middle ages, powder-monkey was the name given to one who brought powder to those who were using a new kind of weapon. That is the whole question. We want to be the peacemakers and not the powder-monkeys in this world. We have had enough of arms dealers.
It would be ridiculous to think that we could find a solution to the whole problem, but the beginning of a solution would occur if we would put into practice the resolutions that were in the United Nations and we have said that we agree to. But no effort has been made by the superpowers to find a homeland for these Palestinians who were pushed out of their land.
There are frustrations among the Arab states. Mind you, there have been a lot of Arab states which use the Palestinians as a political football. I am here as a member of Parliament, not to create enemies.
Where were the Saudis when the Palestinians really needed help? Where was Kuwait? Kuwait is a pure fabrication of a country, with a totally undemocratic system where hundreds of billions of dollars are in the hands of a relatively few people. I am sure the average American must realize that there has to be something drastically wrong when a few families control hundreds of billions of dollars, deposited in American treasury bonds and in American and Swiss banks.
How long is this frustration going to be left to fester in the Middle East, until we have an outbreak of hostilities that will have terrible ramifications? Is it going to be this time, if we can get out of this peaceably, that we will realize that we have to sit down and find the final solution to clear Lebanon of the foreign armies on its soil and find a place for the Palestinians, a right they have under the United Nations Charter, so they will

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
have a place they can call home? Still today there are universities and schools in the occupied territories which have been closed for two years.
That goes against all humanitarian things that we have stood for in the past. Yet, it is permitted to continue. We are expected to jump in line immediately because the Americans wanted to protect oil.
Once again I say: Where were they when Lebanon was overrun? Where were they when the Palestinians were calling out just to have a piece of land that they could call home?
In conclusion, for all those who believe that there is a just solution for the Middle East and in the humanitarian treatment, the place to look to is the United Nations to enforce those resolutions. It is the people in this country who can call upon the government and say that it has been 15 years that the civil war in Lebanon has been permitted to go on.
Since 1948 the Palestinians have not had a place to rest their weary heads. I call upon Canadians to ask simple questions of the Minister of External Affairs or of the government and say: Can we not use our role in the Security Council to say that time has come that these resolutions be respected? That is all we want.
To the government of this country, for the tradition and the respect that we have built up through the many years, we want it to continue, needless to say. We want to be the peacemaker and not the powder-monkey. That should be very clear. To all Canadians maybe it seems frustrating because we feel completely powerless, but we are not.
Our church organizations could be writing to our Prime Minister and to the Minister of External Affairs. If they knew that there were thousands and thousands of Canadians who are aware of the situation, we would see more action.
I was very happy to participate in this debate. It is very hard to stay calm after years of tragedy upon tragedy upon a people who do not deserve to be victims. It is amazing when one looks at the history of that part of the world to see that when the Arabs had their civilization,
there was so little discrimination. It seems ironic that today they would be the victims of such discrimination.

Mr. Speaker, my esteemed colleague just said: "How can I stay calm?"
My comment is: Why should you stay calm when you see so much hypocrisy in North America, especially in Washington and I dare say in Ottawa, Mr. Speaker? How can you remain calm when these young people I see here could be the ones who may be asked to go if things over there turn as I expect most likely and I wish would never take place? How can you remain calm? Why should you remain calm?
My comment to my colleague is when you talk about the Middle East, Mr. Speaker, you have talked about the Middle East in the past. Would you explain to me to help me for my introductory remarks later on maybe. I may decide to give up, because every time you talk about the Middle East either in the Liberal Party of Canada, in the House of Commons of Canada or in any political party, everybody gets dizzy. Mr. Speaker, you can talk about anything in the world, but do not touch the Middle East.
My colleague explained to me his understanding of this nervousness when we start talking about the Middle East. He is a distinguished member of Parliament who sat in the National Assembly in Quebec. He was not defeated. He did not run in 1976. He came back to the Liberal Party of Canada, my party, at a very difficult time, when we were very low in the polls in 1984. He resigned his seat in Quebec City and got elected. He should not apologize for being passionate.
Could he help me out? What is his understanding of the reason why so many people are so nervous in political circles, especially when we want to find in all honesty a solution and justice for all. All means all parties. Would he enlighten me, please?

Mr. Speaker, I am flattered because the hon. member for Saint-Denis is very knowledgeable an international affairs, especially the Middle East. I should be asking him for advice. I am looking forward to hearing his speech later on, and I
October 18, 1990

know it will be very interesting. I would like to say to the hon. member-
There is lots to be upset about.

Agreed. The hon. member is right to be upset. But he made an interesting point. One wonders about the reluctance of members of this House to talk about the Middle East in public. It seems to me that if we have the privilege of being elected and sitting in the House, we should feel no hesitation about saying what we want to say if we are deeply committed. If we don't speak out, people will not respect our opinions. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you understand that if you don't speak up for what you believe in, people won't respect you. I agree. The reason for this reluctance to talk about the Middle East is that they are afraid of a backlash. When we want to talk about the plight of the Palestinians, they are afraid of being accused of anti-semitism. My father was a Semite. Why should I be afraid to speak out when I saw his country being destroyed? This is the place to speak out. Everyone in this House should honestly say what they think about this issue, because if they don't, they don't deserve to be here.
To the hon. member I would like to say that when we stand here in the House, we have the right and the moral obligation to say what we truly think and to defend those who cannot defend themselves. That is what makes them reluctant because they are afraid of being accused of being one thing or another. They might as well go home and let people who do have the courage say what they think.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in what has been a debate that has not only taken place in this auspicious Chamber in the country of Canada, but right across the international community.
It is a debate that has been waged and it is a debate that continues. It is my belief that most Canadians, in my humble estimation, would react in favour with the general response from the international community in response to the blind and naked aggression of Saddam Hussein on behalf of Iraq.
I say that because I believe most people share the general tenor of what has crystalized, if you will, the United Nations on the one hand, a United Nations that is able to mobilize not only one or two or three major
Government Orders
countries or the two superpowers, but in fact a litany of proud sovereign nations which have rallied to that call. They have beckoned their men and women to tiy to stand up for what they believe is in the best interests of that great word we call democracy, which that has many definitions to many different people.
I believe also that in a certain sense many people would probably value the general actions embarked upon by President Bush. It is not often that many Canadians, indeed many parliamentarians and indeed this member of Parliament, would go out of their way to tiy to pay some degree of homage to international leadership by the United States of America. Usually it is on the receiving end. Usually the United States for one reason or another is always subject to criticism, perhaps because sometimes it is the biggest, it is the most powerful, it is the richest, and it is the most influential. Quite often it receives criticism, whether it is from this country or others, in terms of being the popular whipping boy for everyone's concerns.
I do not pretend to be a military expert, nor an expert on the Middle East. One of the most popular words in describing the affairs of the Middle East is the word complicated. It is in everyone's vocabulary. My colleague who just spoke before me eloquently, compassionately, and passionately referred to the word "complicated". I do not pretend to stand in this Chamber as an expert on that part of the world nor on military exercises. In terms of what I hear from my constituents and what I hear in terms of my discussions with Canadians and others, the situation is that if we have not acted-and when I say "we", I mean the international community-where would things be today? If no one would have stood up to Mr. Saddam Hussein, would he be comfortable now in perhaps also having invaded Saudi Arabia?
Would it in fact have destabilized more than it has already the coming together of an international resolve of enormous repercussions and of enormous consequences in the positive light of the speed with which the Soviet Union has had its own economic and political revolution and the speech with which we see the changes in eastern Europe?
If we had not stepped in as an international community, the question of what would have been can never be answered. The answer potentially in some people's minds is a very scary scenario. In general I think the actions of the international community meet with very

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
much favour in this Parliament and in fact across this country.
When we talk about things moving very quickly in eastern Europe or in the Soviet Union, we also have to say that the number of movements in the Middle East has been incredible.
Who would have thought several months ago that an Arab country would have actually publicly invited the United States of America to send troops on its soil? Who would have thought that Saudi Arabia would have permitted 100,000, 150,000 or 200,000 troops on its soil to defend not only sovereignty but to do so against another Arab country? Who would have thought of it back in May or June? Who would have thought that Syria would have been fighting side by side with Americans boys and women, when in fact several years ago the Syrians were targeted by the Americans and other in the sense of being one of the culprits for international destabilization and acts of terrorism? Today they are fighting side by side. Who would have thought that Egypt as well would have been participating and giving the green light to the Americans to do what they are doing today?
When we speak of changes in eastern Europe and in the Soviet Union, we also have to recognize that there have been great changes in the Middle East as well. Changes come and changes go. Friendships are made and friendships are broken. Allies are convened and alliances are disposed of as well. While I generally welcome the unity of Arabs together with the Americans and the international community, I also caution Canada and the United States not to forget and dispose of the long trusted alliances that we have seen between Canada and the United States in that part of the region.
Israel is a perfect case in hand. Israel is by no means perfect, like Canada, like the United States, and like every other country. My good friend who spoke before me talked about truth. He talked about deception. He talked about lies. Who knows where that truth lies.
I do not think we should fall into the trap that Mr. Hussein tried to set for the international community in suggesting somehow it was evil Israel that was behind the Americans doing what they are doing, that somehow it was flying by disguise in American planes. We should not fall into the trap of a leader who was desperate to regain
his foothold in the Arab communities he had lost. Nothing more unites a number of the Arab countries than that word called Israel.
We also have to recognize that we have alliances with that country and have had them for a long time. We also have to recognize when my hon. friend speaks of freedoms and democracies that it also happens to be the only democracy in that part of the world, the only democracy that has a forum like this one, where deputies can get up and debate the issues of the day, the only place where people have a vote.
I do not see this aggression as an aggression by the Iraqi people necessarily. I see it as an aggression by one individual who I think sees a lot of potential glory for himself. There probably is a great deal of trouble underground with this man called Hussein in his own country.
How long did it take the Soviet Union to change? How long and how many leaders have we had to go through for the Soviets now to enjoy a bit of the democracy that we enjoy every day and take so much for granted? It was not until Gorbachev came along and gave some power back to the people. Now he has his problems as a consequence of democracy, but they are better problems than the problems of totalitarian regimes.
That is also the situation in the Middle East-military regimes and dictatorships. When I see the new alliances I see that things are changing, but I also say that we should be very careful not to dispose of old alliances. Israel has been an alliance and Israel has been a friend, and we should continue to be.
Despite the fact that the Palestinian question should be uppermost in any agenda facing the international community, no one doubts for one moment the urgency of any peoples in that country to have a homeland, to have a place they could call home. However, it would be too simple to cast blame only on one side and not look at the realities of the other. The refugee camps in the West Bank are still in existence. We should also be mindful of the fact that those same refugee camps existed when it was under Jordanian rule. When Jordan had the West Bank they were still Palestinian refugee camps. When the Jordanians governed that part of the country which is now under occupied territories, there was not one
October 18, 1990

university. There are now six. There were not the opportunities of work that there are now.
We talk about the truth. We talk about historical forces. We talk about manipulation. Also we should recognize that the Palestinian question also unfortunately serves the political agenda of certain Palestinian and Arabic leaders, but the people who lose are the young, the old, and the Palestinians who go without a home. The situation is not so simple that we can cast blame on one side and ignore the realities of history and the reality of present circumstances. While there are changes we should also keep in mind the alliances that have stood firm through the test of time and through the test of challenges.
In terms of the Canadian participation let me first salute the men and women who are presently in the gulf. These Canadians are acting on behalf of this country and symbolically acting with the world. I salute them this evening because they merit saluting. There is no greater service to one's country than through our Armed Forces and those who defend the country.
I like every other member of Parliament have people within my riding who are serving in the forces. I have 83 such Canadians in my federal riding of York West. When we go down the list of their names it really speaks boldly and proudly about this place Canada. They are people like Staliano, Ross, Sala, Rosenberger, Samute, and Sigh. They are all Canadians, regardless of their cultural backgrounds, all Canadian Armed Forces personnel from the riding of York West who are now in the Middle East.
I believe that there are two things that need to be said about the process by which this Prime Minister has led the forces in the Middle East and in the gulf. The first one is the uneasy feeling that people have about the fact that the voyage departed before UN concurrence was obtained. There was a very uneasy feeling among many Canadians. Despite their feelings as to what Mr. Hussein was trying to do, they were uneasy because they did not like the idea of losing any independence that we had on the international stage or the idea of trying to be subservient to the President of the United States when he beckoned our Prime Minister to the United States.
Government Orders
I believe there was some discomfort because it did not show the patience and the strength of trying to provide on day one a mission that was sanctioned, that was given the political green light under the auspices of the United Nations, which I am proud to say has always been the mark of past Liberal Prime Ministers when asked to serve.
The second aspect of the process, as opposed to the substance, was that this country and this Parliament was kept completely in the dark, as many members have said before me. The American President met with his Congressional leaders. He went on national TV to talk to Americans in their living rooms. He held daily briefings for the media of that country and was able from his golf cart to suggest the latest, even though I disagreed with that kind of image politics that everyone read through.
Where was our Prime Minister, in comparison? Did he speak to the opposition parties? Did he consult opposition leaders? Did he contact CBC and CTV to try to broadcast into the living rooms of Canadians from coast to coast? Did he offer daily media briefings so that we could at least communicate with each other? No, he did not.
I know he had a barbecue in Washington. I know he came back to his residence and everything was secret. The Minister of National Defence was called in. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was leaving, but Canadians were left wondering where was Parliament, the forum of national debate.
Why was Parliament not recalled? There was no debate. There was no discussion. There was no attempt at one resolution so that we could speak as one voice, offer a political resolution to the House of Commons and speak internationally for a change, rather than try to divide and conquer domestically. Several years ago, the Prime Minister realized that 174 people who arrived on the east coast one fine summer constituted a national crisis. When we allow 200,000 immigrants a year, when we allowed 100,000 Vietnamese boat people in 1980, all of a sudden 174 people constitute a crisis. What was his response after he falsely said it was for a crisis he called an emergency sitting of this Parliament? Can you imagine anything more despicable, more manipulative and anything more misleading in your lifetime? I cannot. The Prime Minister was low in the polls then and tried to step up those polls by stepping on the so-called refugees. He is low in the polls again today. Rather than having

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
manipulated a false crisis, his responsibility ought to have been to react to a real crisis this summer, which he failed to do.
The Prime Minister had to stop the ships off the coast of Sicily because they were getting to the gulf too early. If they arrived there too early it would have triggered an earlier debate in the House of Commons. What an embarrassment it was to stop our ships midstream because the Prime Minister did not have the courage to face Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, you rightfully indicate my time is up. There is much which this Prime Minister and this government have to face. He is fortunate that he has been embraced in the sense that the international community has acted, but he should have done it like the other countries where Britain, France, Italy and countless others had the courage to take their people into their confidence and in a time of crisis unite them and stand united. That was not the case in this country and we are proud today in spite of this Prime Minister and in spite of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very straightforward question for the member who just spoke, the chair of the Liberal caucus. There were discussions earlier in the debate about the possibility of another motion being put forward.
A Liberal member for one of the Toronto ridings indicated that he would be prepared to support the terms of that motion which the government sought to introduce. I wonder if the member who just spoke could indicate what position he will take with respect to the resolution now on the Order Paper to be voted on. Does the hon. member intend to vote for or against that
motion in the event that the amendments on the Order Paper are not adopted?

Mr. Speaker, my message, to paraphrase another great Canadian, is just watch us. I think he should just have patience. I believe that in the finest traditions of the House we, in the Liberal Party, have no apologies to make whatsoever in trying to galvanize a unified solitary voice emanating from this Parliament.
Because the Prime Minister was incapable of putting a motion before us that would speak to that, because he did not recall Parliament, we saw and felt the need among Canadians in terms of their aspirations of wanting some leadership. We have discussed with various parties in this Chamber the possibility of having a motion that truly speaks to the greatness of this country, its ambitions and aspirations. We will continue those discussions.
We take no lessons from a New Democratic Party that has very little credibility when it comes to defence matters and very little credibility when it comes to NATO. We used to have the former leaders talking about pulling out of NATO. That was when the NDP was unpopular. Do you remember those days?
All of sudden, for a short span of time back in 1987, Ed Broadbent jumped to the top of the polls. Then they asked him what the NDP policy was on NATO. This is when he was very popular. He said he might not contemplate pulling out of NATO in the first year of their term of office. I realize where my hon. friend is coming from and I realize where he is trying to go. Before he tries to talk to the Liberal Party he should realize that neither he nor his party has a monopoly on virtue, let alone defence.

the event that the amendment for which they negotiated, which was supposed to take the place of these other amendments is not introduced? Also, what will the NDP do on the main motion and on the Liberal motion?

Mr. Speaker, my friend from Eglinton- Lawrence asks a very interesting question. Perhaps indirectly, he answers the question of my hon. friend from Burnaby. I must be honest with my friend from Eglinton-Lawrence. I do not know from one day to the next what the New Democratic Party is going to do or what it stands for. If you recall last week when their House leader, on a Thursday evening, made his maiden speech in the Senate. He called it tyranny.
The next day, Friday morning in Question Period, the House leader suggested that the Senate does not work and it should be abolished. One cannot have it both ways. That is the fallacy that underlies many of the pronouncements and many of the policies of the New Democratic Party.
My friend from Eglinton-Lawrence will now have a chance to see what the New Democratic Party is all about in the province of Ontario. I noticed the remarks made by the member for Eglinton-Lawrence on post interviews of what happened. He quite rightly pointed to a long list of commitments and promises made by the New Democratic Party. The sixty-four thousand dollar question is, will they keep those and at what cost? I must be honest. The New Democratic Party confuses me from day to day. I am not sure where they are going to be Monday because today is still Thursday.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a comment while my colleague from Toronto is speaking. I am sure it is an inadvertent comment because these are very important facts. I know that some people in the world would like us to say what he said. I am sure he did not mean it. I consulted with my friend, the admiral of the fleet of the Liberal Party from Newfoundland. First, I did not know it was a debate on Israel or I would have adjusted my speech but it is too late. Second, he called the state of Israel our ally and friend.
Government Orders
It has to be corrected. It is important to correct it, because the meaning of ally means more than a friend. Israel is a friend of Canada, but we are not an ally. It is not our ally. I stand to be corrected, but the military implication that suddenly Canada is an ally of that friendly country called Israel would be immense. I am sure he does not want us to drag Canada's youth into the problems of the Middle East.

Mr. Speaker, speakers before me more eloquently talked about the Palestinians and the Palestinian question.
There have been a lot of comments about the Middle East. How the member who is a noted internationalist would speak of the Middle East by only speaking of the Palestinians without the state of Israel is a debate that will never start.
I also referred in this context to the fact that Syria right now happens to be an ally. Egypt happens to be an ally in the situation of the gulf. I make no apologies for what I said. I consider Israel a friend and an ally. I repeat that for the record.

Mr. Speaker, my comment will be very short.

Mr. Speaker, the former Prime Minister that the member alluded to will go down in the annals of history as one of the greatest prime ministers who ever governed this country. I do not say that easily, because there have been a great many tremendous men who have come before him and no doubt will follow.
Certainly, in terms of the comment that alluded to a previous time, that too enjoyed tremendous public opinion and favour.
This was a former Prime Minister who enjoyed not only the respect of Liberally-minded individuals, but in
talking to average Canadians, whether they disagreed with Liberal policies or not, there was a certain respect for that individual that transcended the abilities and the attempts by the current regime to be loved by all people, including this gentleman's party. We will continue, as I said, to strive for oneness and to speak with one voice, aided by one great speaker.

Mr. Speaker, in 1964, I happily made a big decision. I wanted to get into federal politics by running for a federal seat. I was involved in politics ever since I could remember. I was supposed to run for the Quebec Liberal Party in 1960, but I agreed to yield my seat to the hon. Rene Levesque. I had a passion for politics and a passion for my country. A passion for my country, meaning Canada. And I say it in French: "La passion de mon pays, le Canada". I also felt that a federal member had to be concerned about provincial matters, about families, the elderly, the needy, the handicapped and those unable to defend themselves. We must understand that in Canada, people are different. Mr. Speaker, I like you and I respect you, but your cultural background is different from mine. So I tried to understand inter-parliamentary and inter-provincial relations.
My second reason for getting into federal politics was my great interest in international politics. I demonstrated this at the University of Ottawa by organizing a demonstration against the racist policies of Governor Faubus of Arkansas. I don't have any notes, it's not in my notes. We burned him in effigy at the University of Ottawa. That resulted in hundreds and thousands of protests and congratulations from all across United States. Why? Because a reporter who knew me was there, covering the news for the international media. This caused a lot of problems with the authorities at Ottawa U which at the time was run by the Oblate Fathers. Attracting attention was a no-no. We always had to conform.

You were not allowed to dare-

I always like to-
October 18, 1990



I always loved to dare to be different in international politics. I know many of my colleagues seem to be friendly to me and I appreciate this very much. Our young colleague in the NDP, for whom I have great esteem for his brightness, his energy, and his courage, has tried to divide us. He knows I do not play that kind of politics. That is the only place where I will disagree with him-trying to say that there was blood in caucus yesterday morning. There was no blood. If there were blood, I would be the one who would be bloody.

Yesterday, emotions ran high, but this evening I will try to be at least outwardly calm.
I am going to tell you, without actually doing so, what happened in caucus. Yesterday, I explained more or less what had motivated me throughout my life: my country, Canada-it seems it isn't very popular right now to say this in Quebec but I am going to say it anyway and my abiding interest in international problems.
Even when you are misunderstood and harassed and blackmailed, you have to stand up to defend your views, while respecting those of colleagues who do not share them.
I watched the debate this evening. It was about everything except the debate. There is a motion. It's not very complicated. To Canadians who are going to listen to this, let me explain that we have a government motion that was amended by my party-I repeat, my party-the Liberal Party of Canada, and again amended by the New Democratic Party.
Well, I have read and I support the NDP amendment. I didn't think twice about it. And I will tell you why. Of course, as a member of this party, I have not really had a chance to disagree, but my time will come. However, I support the amendment presented by our competent new External Affairs critic. He is brilliant, intelligent, but always uneasy when the subject is the Middle East, like anyone else, like me and like the others. But he is brilliant and intelligent, and he has his heart in the right place. I hope to win him over on the Middle East.
So I intend to vote for that motion. But I cannot vote in favour of the government's motion. In any case, my colleagues- At least, not for the motion before the House, and as for a future motion, I haven't heard about
Government Orders
it, because this is all going on behind the scenes. Some members are consulted, others aren't. Imagine! I say this for the benefit of those listening because I intend to ask my friends to review my speech-I told them about it-because for me, this is a very demanding debate. So I will try to be very calm as I prefer to be on these serious occasions.
What really upsets me, and that is why I intend to defend the amendment of the Liberal Party of Canada, and so I should, because it condemns the government for not having recalled Parliament. And I think that is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker.
In 1986, Parliament was recalled for a minor incident, compared to what might happen in the Middle East-it was about the Parole Board. In 1987, Mr. Benoit Bouchard said: "Parliament has been recalled-

-to deal with an issue of great national importance. [Translation]
At issue were a few miserable Tamil refugees in Nova Scotia. The nation in an uproar! Canadian racism! People were horrified because these refugees probably did not have the same colour of skin as my friend from Toronto or my own- people often tell me that if they had been Poles or Germans or people like that, there wouldn't have been this uproar in Canada. However, the government was up in arms and Parliament was recalled. I found that positively horrifying.
An international crisis is in the making, and the Government refuses to call back Parliament. That is what the Liberal amendment is about. We won't recall Parliament because it's nothing serious. Nothing serious at all. We are going to send young Canadians-first three ships, three ships which my eminent colleague, Admiral Fred Mifflin, had under his command-we start with three. The great Canadian contribution, in answer to the call of warriors Bush and Thatcher! We are doing our bit for the war effort.
But this is not enough, because if you send three ships you need someone to defend those ships. So we are sending 18 CFs to protect our ships. But there is more. I hope everybody is listening very carefully. We also had to send several hundred people to take care of these planes. And there isn't a war on yet. There is no conflict.

October 18, 1990

I said earlier that in my student days I organized a demonstration against Orval Faubus. In 1957,1 set up the National Welcome Committee and I was a student coordinator when we received the Hungarians who came to Canada, who had left their country and who went as far as Vancouver. There was a reception in every city. Later, in 1968,1 was a member of Parliament, and I was involved and went to take a look personally in Czechoslovakia. I defended and protected U.S. draft dodgers. There is an American book on the subject, and I was surprised to see it was written in 1970, and the title is The New Exile.

I wish you would read it. There are just two or three pages that tell what I did, because others could not do it. It states that the man the hon. member mentioned, one of my ex-leaders, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, could not do so. I was used willingly, because the caucus was divided. It seems we are always divided on great questions. It is all right. That means vitality. Maybe it is a speech of return that I am making, but I want to show consistency. That is why I am trying to enumerate, not to be pompous. I hope people who know me know that I do not give a damn. But I want to show that I have always had that commitment of daring and of consistency.
I was a delegate, appointed by Pierre Elliott Trudeau, at the United Nations in 1974 when Arafat said: "Please listen to me. Don't let me down." The western world, instead of listening, boycotted Arafat. I am the only one who stood up. I was blamed by the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, but Trudeau did not recall me from the United Nations.
But I paid a hell of price, my dear friends. I do not mind. We should have listened to that voice in 1974 that was saying: "Please don't let me down." Remember what happened in Lebanon in 1976, and on, and on. Again, it is this refusal of being there at the right time, instead of waiting for contamination and then finding a solution.
Of course, this invasion of Kuwait by Saddam Hussein is unacceptable. I have met Saddam Hussein. I spoke in the Parliament of Kuwait. That was before the Emir disbanded the parliament because he did not like it too much. Perhaps it was going too fast. Of course, I
condemn that, but let us go back to the source. The young people today would like to benefit from the dividends of peace. Have we forgotten who gave him the best of arms and arms-

Well, I know and Quebecers know that despite its competences our army certainly does not have all the sophisticated weaponry that the super and intermediate powers were fighting to sell to Iran or Irak for eight years, to Israel and Syria- I name them all because they are all countries to me. And today, it seems to come as a shock, as an insult or just as a surprise to some people suddenly to discover that Saddam Hussein is a great military man. The military strength of Hussein is incredible. But who armed him to the teeth in the first place? We did! That is a fact.
So there is a question we must answer. I was saying that as a proud French Canadian, for which I insist there is no translation-

I am a Canadian frangais. There is no translation for that.

But with an abiding concern for international affairs, I said to myself: What would Canada's role be in this kind of crisis? And that, hon. members is why I am disappointed in this government which failed to take advantage of Canada's extraordinary reputation throughout the world, which did not know what Canadians want-

What Canadians want is not to say yes, Mrs. Thatcher, yes, Mr. Mitterrand, yes, Mr. Bush. It is to be that kind of country where you have the Marchi, the Comuzzi, the Volpe, the Prud'homme and the Paproski. This is the kind of country that could be so exciting. What kind of international role can that country play? What role can it play at the United Nations? Have you seen any nervousness of this cabinet?
Mario Andreotti is my master of international politics. He writes to me, could you believe that? Ask Mr. Bevilacqua. He used to read the message to me because it is in Italian and he writes so small. But he is my master
October 18, 1990

in international politics. He is working hard. Mitterrand, he is working hard.
Let me ask a small permission. As long as I am not too attacking, I am sure I will get it. What I would like to know of my colleagues, Canadians, do we really reflect the kind of action Canada can better play than to send, with all due respect, three ships and 18 planes? Is that not what Canadians really would prefer even though people see how Gallup last night says 58 per cent approve of the government's action, so we all get excited. We say we cannot vote against the motion, 58 per cent. It may be 38 tomorrow, and maybe 12 if war starts and we lose young Canadians who could have been used otherwise diplomatically. And I will tell you why. Canada is one of the few countries that already has Canadians over there.
The Associate Minister of National Defence, a gracious woman, nice lady, nice member of Parliament, said she felt great last night for these 900 and 500, but I feel equally great, my friend from Toronto who is listening so intently. He thinks I am going to explode. I will surprise him.
We have hundreds of young Canadians on the Golan Heights. We do not talk about that. The pride of Canada, Mr. Speaker, a hundred young Canadians, young Canadian girls and boys are in Cyprus. They are the pride of Canada for our reputation.
My colleagues, I could speak for hours. I prepare myself accordingly. Do you know how many resolutions there are on the Cyprus question, asking ask Turkey to get out of Cyprus that it has occupied 40 per cent since 1974? Have you ever mentioned that? Have you ever heard about that? No, as someone would say, there is no oil there.

200,000 refugees out of a population of 600,000, and we do nothing, we say nothing. We have young Canadians on the border between Iran and Irak, we have young Canadians in the Sinai. What kind of role do you think Canada will be able to play tomorrow, hon. members? of course, there is the economic blockade. We are helping to enforce. It was a UN decision. I support that decision. We support it. This military aspect, is that Canada's calling? I say no. How many countries now contributing to this major military effort are also considered to be

supportive of UN contingents? Few. Examine, look around! All of a sudden we have a crisis on our hands. I am very glad that the United Nations should experience such renewed vigour, despised as they are by the Americans who still owe them in excess of $500 million. The United Nations may have to close the shop. Then overnight there is a world out there because the Soviet Union is falling apart, they are no longer a dangerous military power, so now there is no problem. Good. But we will have to respect all United Nations resolutions, not just some of them. Those of Cyprus. Go and ask-
Go and ask your friends of Greek and Cypriot origin, numbering some 200,000 in Toronto, if Marcel Prud'h-omme is a kook in defending the importance of respecting the United Nations resolution on Cyprus. Ask them in Toronto and Montreal. I know the answer.
