I will not be provocative. I thank the House.
There have been a multiplicity of resolutions on the Middle East by the hundreds. The United States used its veto 20 times. I could go on and on, but because the House has been indulgent, I will not abuse the privilege.
Tonight I could have been negative. But as most of my colleagues know there is a little something in me that says even if I am outraged about something, I still prefer to try not to go the anger route, but try to convince people that this country, so beautiful to work and live in, has such a great role to play in the world. I am not going to beg to do that on my two knees because I come from-

-the Province of Quebec and I am a French Canadian. Never will I go down on my knees before the rest of Canada to defend my views because to me that is only part and parcel of what Canada is.
I could have talked to you about this newspaper-

October 18, 1990
Government Orders

The Suburban, Montreal. So, I will be positive, I will only attract attention. If people want to know what they write about me, every Quebecer, Canadien frangais, knows about that paper. The Suburban, Wednesday, October 17, page A5. I am told that is one good way I am told to attract attention. Please read that. The Suburban is a sick paper from west Island Montreal.

But like Gorbachev once said here in Parliament, while dogs bark the caravan goes by. So I would rather not comment on that. But all I am asking, dear colleagues-I wish there were more of you, I realize that international affairs wear people down, so before I tire you out and abuse I want to assure you that I deeply regret the fact that the government did not see fit to recall Parliament for an emergency debate. That is the resolution of the Liberal Party, of the Official Opposition, to censure the government for failing to recall the House. I will vote in favour. We should not wrap ourselves in the flag of the United Nations- Not the United States. I have nothing, I am pro-American. I do not like their foreign policy in the Middle East. That is all I am a very civilized man. As neighbours go, they are terrific, but I do not want to take orders from the United States. If this is a United Nations mission we will take our responsibilities.
I know-and I will end on this note, Mr. Speaker- that a catch-all resolution is being drafted so that all members might vote with a clear conscience.
Because, in conclusion, I must say that some people have been very nervous over the past week. Because they do not want to discuss the real issues in the Middle-East, they do not want to get to the bottom of things. My colleague from Gatineau-La Lievre did so in such a brilliant manner. We must get to the roots of the larger problem.
But remember that on October 29, 1947, my country- [English]
-your country, my colleagues, November 29, 1947, voted at the United Nations to create two states on Palestinian land, by a vote of 13-10. I think I know my facts very well.
Why do we not finish that job too? Do not be afraid of those who talk about linkage. I heard colleagues say: "We must not have any linkage", as if these things are not links. We must have that first. Fine. Let us solve that one.
But we must also be prepared, and announce ahead of time, that immediately upon having finished solving the Iraq-Kuwait issue, it should be well known internationally that there will be as much devotion and passion in the world community.
We should first solve what is going on in the Middle East. Then Marcel Prud'homme will be the happiest person because he will have the same devotion to his country and, hopefully, to international affairs. But do not ask me to be someone else in my country. I will always be myself. I have as much pride as anybody else.
I have much interest in world affairs, and I think that this government will find it unusual to hear me speaking so vigorously against the government. I think that the government has failed me-of course when I say me, I mean Canada- on this particular issue by not using this opportunity to see what all of us, together, the Marchis, the Comuzzis, the Mifflins, the Robinsons, the Prud'-hommes, the Paproskis can do to see if there is not something different, if there is not a role that could be different for Canada at the United Nations and in this crisis.
That is why I will vote for the motion. I am a responsible person. That is why I will vote for the amendment. That is why I will vote against the motion of that government because I am against it.
I am told now that there is a surprise coming. Well, my commitment at the moment is to vote yes, yes and no, and wait for the surprise, but I hope some people will take me in their confidence. As the oldest parliamentarian, I can only smell that there is something going on, but everything is escaping me. I almost live in this Parliament, so it is very difficult to escape me because I am devoted to see what kind of country we want and what kind of role we can play in world affairs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

October 18, 1990

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for his excellent speech and especially for the courage he has demonstrated on this issue. I know full well that he has had to pay a very high price within his party for the courage he has shown from the very beginning on this major issue, demanding justice for the Palestinians. I know he has paid and continue to pay a very high price within his party, and I wish once again to congragulate him for his courage and the fact that he has always stated his mind on this issue of justice for the Palestinians. Mr. Speaker, he was attacked recently in a degusting manner in The Suburban.
I have two very straightforward questions for the hon. member. My first question is with respect to the position of the Liberal Party on this issue. I know my hon. friend does not necessarily speak for the party on this question, but perhaps he could clarify for the House the position of the Liberal Party-a party of which he has been a member for many years-with respect to the question of an international conference on the Middle East, a conference including all parties affected, as well as representatives of the Palestinians, which dealing with the issue of self-determination may very well lead to the creation of an independent state for the Palestinians side by side with a secure Israel.
Second, my question concerns the motion discussed by some members in the House and referred to by the hon. member for York West, the motion which the government attempted to put to this House a couple of days ago to which the hon. member for St. Denis objected at that point because quite properly from his perspective he had not been given notice. What is his position with respect to the substance of that motion? Does he support that motion as his colleague from Davenport and others have indicated, or does he oppose that motion?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate, and I talk to you as I have always talked to you privately, as a young friend. I find you bright, articulate, devoted and sincere. But, please, on this important issue, I hope that you are not trying to show that there is division in the Liberal Party. There is strong opinion in the Liberal Party on this
Government Orders
question, but to me the subject matter is so important that I am not interested in showing there is division.
I am glad to report to you that ten years ago, or five, six, four, or three, we talked about international conferences and it was unacceptable. I am glad. I do not want to take any credit for anything any more in this House. I have not sat in this party yet, but I think we are moving there. So, I have little reason to rejoice.
Yes, I think it has to be accepted. I hope there will be a debate and I will then throw you the book. Give me two hours, and I will get out. I am even ready in two hours to get out of the House on this issue. I mean it, every second of it. I have paid too much in my emotion, my blood and my thinking to stand up for the damn thing because I am convinced it is in the interests of world humanity that we address the question of the Middle East as a whole.
Second, I will give you my position. I do not think it is the role of Canada to send troops. I will see what they say on Monday. They may know more than I on this resolution. I was not consulted. What I have to defend is what I read and what I read is that we will most likely vote on that. If it is like that, yes to your amendment, yes to our amendment, and no to the government motion. If others want to vote differently we will see what they come up with, but I will be surprised if they will get my support.

Mr. Speaker, it is true that the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis has always shown great courage; he has always stated his mind and always been consistent. It is also true that he has paid a high price for his convictions, but he was not afraid.
As he said-I am coming to my question-how does he manage-? He has always been recognized, and he often tells me: "I am a French-Speaking Canadian and proud of it!" God knows that he is recognized as such. Moreover, he has always spoken out against the fact that the United Nations and the major powers have never helped Cyprus against the Turks who raped the island.
Being a proud Canadian and pro French-Canadian has he ever been accused of being against English Canada? Never! I have never heard that.

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
Has he ever been accused of being against the Turks? Never! How is it, then, that when he tries to defend the interests of Palestinians or those who suffer in the Middle East, he is accused of being antisemitist? Could the hon. member explain that? How is it possible? You have been categorized in the Suburban, but I have never seen a Toronto newspaper accuse you of being against

I will be very cool on that- [Translation]
For me, as a French Canadian, it is natural. Any human being belong to a corner of the earth.

I will do it in English. Yes, I am Canadien frangais but I hope its for life. You understand that, but you have to feel at home. I have never known anybody since I have belonged to this country, in my country I am not recognized. I am not equal, so-

I am a French Canadian, but I am a Quebecer first, that is clear. Personally I have no problem. I know that tomorrow some people will say: He has defended Canada. It is not true! I said that I will never kneel in front of anybody, because I have my pride. But I recognize also that my friend Comuzzi has his pride, just as my friend Mifflin.
The second? My God, it is so provocating that I would rather pass.

In the spirit that we have developed tonight, I would not answer the second one. I will not, I regret. But I will make another statement for The Suburban, that doggy newspaper-I do not even know bad words in English, and preserve the House that I use the one in French. Just to conclude, I will not answer that except, and I am not afraid to say this, I have always said and it is on record in the House of Commons that anti-Semitism is a cancer. Do you understand what this means?

Antisemitism is a cancer which eats up the inside.

But how many times do I have to repeat that? I never receive any flattering article by the Canadian Jewish Congress or the Zionists of Canada and yet Marcel Prud'homme, Canadien frangais montrealais time and time and time again, for 25 years, has always said that. There is nothing worse than anti-Semitism because it eats you from the inside. Once you allow your heart, your passion, your head to become anti-Semitic you have opened the door to yourself to be anti-black, anti-Catholic, anti-everything you do not like. So how do I still feel so healthy? But I understand the passion of the people they want to defend. It is their problem. They should understand that the greatest friends of Israel are not necessarily their blind friends because their blind friends may not help that state to survive.
People like me, and I say it seriously, can do a hell of a lot more to say to people: "Hey, buster, that country exists. Canada voted for it. That country has the right to exist but like every other country, but the other one has the right to exist". I know it is a perpetual debate. If you want to know more, I conclude by a quote. Why do you not read a fantastic book. Parliamentarians, I will send all of you who are here tonight a copy free. I will pay for it. It is entitled They Dare to Speak Out written by an American parliamentarian. He explains what the outcome is all about in that book.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on my respected colleague's speech. I had originally planned to ask the question my colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway asked, which brought to mind the following quote from La Fontaine, a French poet from the Renaissance:
Flatterers laugh at the expense of those who listen to them.
I am very proud of my colleague from Saint-Denis for not listening.
The point I want to make in this debate tonight is that the hon. member for Saint-Denis touched on two themes which unfortunately come back often in our debates. One is passion for this country, an emotion all the hon. members must respect because, in our state-
October 18, 1990

merits, speeches and questions, we always talk about the interest of Canada, and not that of other countries.
The French language, Mr. Speaker, is a wonderful tool to express passions. I note that my friend said, and this is the second time I hear him say it: "I am a Canadian, yes, but French Canadian." The English language is not as precise. Blame it on the structure of the language. In French, Canadian always comes first. The second word acts as a modifier introducing an idea without cancelling out the others. Speaking with heat, my colleague also touched on a second theme: in this House, given the parliamentary system set up by the Canadians, it is always allowed to express dissenting views, because all the hon. members always put up with differences of opinions. Within certain limits, with your permission, Mr. Speaker! There are opinions we can respect without sharing them. I respect my colleague's position and I am glad that he made his position clear to our colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway on the motion debated tonight. It is a positive stance for the Liberal Party.

In either case, whether he goes too far or whether he did not go far enough.
I was here, and I had this opportunity to participate. I decided I would do so after listening to his very eloquent contribution to this debate.
As someone who has watched this Chamber for a long time and hearing the hon. member speak with the passion which he did and delivering the address he did to the House tonight, I could not help but think back to days when I sat in the gallery of this House as a student in the sixties. The hon. member was a member of this House then.
He has been a member of this House continuously since that time. For well over 25 years he has served in this place. It is an enviable record, and one of very distinguished service to Canada in his efforts to ameliorate the condition of hundreds of Canadians as the member of Parliament for Saint-Denis.

I am very pleased to convey to him my congragulations because his impassioned speech was very good. As he said, when one has conviction, one must have passion. That is fine.

Of course, I also listened with some amusement to the questions put by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway. I must say I share the words of the hon. member for Saint-Denis in describing him as erudite and clever. I am sorry that he has taken it upon himself to try to sow seeds of division in the members of this Liberal Party.
He is shaking his head and suggesting that it is not so. Words speak for themselves, and I am sorry that he is trying to be mischievous this evening. I would have expected better of him. Someone as eloquent and as capable as he is, I would have thought might have felt happier in the Liberal Party than in the New Democratic Party.

October 18, 1990
Government Orders
We have tremendous tolerance for varying viewpoints. One of the strongest points of the Liberal Party-I have watched it for a very long time-is its ability to open itself and embrace people of a great variety of opinions and views. The hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway, instead of trying to accept that that is the fact, is busy trying to suggest that somehow because these views can all be accommodated in this great party, somehow a wedge needs to be driven in to drive some members out.
I suggest that it is unworthy of the hon. member. I would suggest that in future he try to contain his enthusiasm for wedge driving, and stick with fair questions that seek to elicit genuine information rather than these efforts to make people feel uncomfortable in the convictions that they hold.
Certainly, the members of this party are encouraged by the example of our string of distinguished leaders, and by the leadership of the party generally to hold their convictions.
The Liberal Party is in fact the party of individual rights. It believes in the worth of the individual, and it accepts differences of opinion. I ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway to bear that in mind when he presses his mischievous questions.
What I wanted to speak about tonight was something of some considerably grave concern, because I think the situation that we are faced with in dealing with this motion is one that arose out of a lengthy summer adjournment that this government foisted upon the House, and really upon the country.
I think it is fair to say that Canadians all across Canada were appalled when this crisis in the Middle East erupted. Indeed, there was another crisis as Your Honour will recall at Oka when the government, despite repeated calls from the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier who is House leader for this party, for the recall of Parliament at an early date to deal with these matters, stonewalled and refused.
This motion is the result of the government's reluctant recall of Parliament. It had to do it, because we had adjourned until September 24. To show that it was really serious about this, it introduced this motion on the first day back. It was debated for a day, and the government expressed some surprise that it did not immediately pass.
Apparently one day was supposedly enough to discuss this important issue. So, they called it another day, and at the end of the day, they said: "How long do you want? Why is this going on so long?" They gave notice of closure. They have never in fact imposed it, but they did come and say we are going to use it unless we get some kind of deal. Now we are sitting late to deal with this issue and we have co-operated in that. We have agreed to sit late in order to allow members who wanted to speak on this issue to do so. I am sorry that the government regards this as so unimportant that four days of debate, strung out over a period of weeks, is enough for the members of Parliament to express the views of their constituents on this very important issue.
I can think back to 1956 when the government of the day was faced with a crisis in the Suez. There was an immediate recall of Parliament to deal with the crisis. Parliament was called into special session. There was a Speech from the Throne and everything. A special session was held so that the members of Parliament could be present and discuss what the Canadian government was doing in an emergency world situation.
We were confronted with a situation that was just as grave, just as serious for world peace this summer. This government did nothing. It twiddled its thumbs and did nothing. It said we will send troops abroad, we will make our decisions but we do not need to call Parliament together. We do not need to discuss this with representatives of the people. We do not need to call the Leader of the Opposition. We do not need to speak to anybody. We will simply talk to the President of the United States, as my hon. friend from Thunder Bay-Nipigon has suggested.
We can talk to the President of the United States. If he says we should send troops, then we will send them. It was a deplorable approach to diplomacy and to the Canadian people. It was contemptuous of Parliament and an insult to the peoples' representatives here.
What the government is doing is exhibiting a pattern of contempt. As someone who appreciates this place and believes that the House of Commons is where matters should be discussed and disposed of, I am appalled at the record of contempt that is shown by the government throughout the two years I have been here. I know the hon. member for Saint-Denis with his 26 years of
4-;


experience could list far more than I could of the way this government has acted in its contemptuous fashion. I can think of a few items that indicate a similar approach to the House of Commons. The failure to call Parliament back this summer is only one. There has been closure used constantly in this House, more than all the other Parliaments in Canadian history put together. That is how often closure has been used in this Parliament. We have had time allocation used in this Parliament time after time. We had the government House leader on his feet the other day saying that in the six years it has been in office, it has used it as many times as the Liberal government had before. I do not think that is much of a record. When you add in the closure use, it is a much more impressive and debilitating record. It shows a tremendous contempt for Parliament.
There are regular lengthy adjournments. You would think that if it was using closure it is because it is jammed with work. But it is not. It uses closure, closure, closure. Then it says, okay, it is time to go home now early and have a long holiday. Do not come back too soon. It asks for extended periods off. We left early in June, we came back late in September. Last year we were off until an extra couple of weeks in January. The year before, we had an extended break. It would not call us back at all until after April 3, I think, in 1989, after a two week session in December. All through the December session in 1988 it used closure at every stage to get it all through in two weeks time.
There is a pattern of contempt and disrespect for Parliament of a constant unwillingness to meet the opposition to deal with us in this Chamber. Why? It is fear. The government members are afraid to face the music that is put to them by us in the opposition. They are afraid to listen to the voices of the people. The evidence of that is in the string of unpopular policies that it pursues when we are not here and when we are here. It says we do not really care whether you want to change this bill. We really do not care if you like our policies. We are going ahead with them anyway. Shut up. If you do not shut up we will put closure on you and shut you up. If that is not enough we will send you away for a long holiday so you really have not got a platform in Parliament to speak on. That is what is going on here and that is what went on in this case. Here we have the govern-

ment choose to send troops abroad. There was a two-week delay while the ships were outfitted. Parliament could easily have been recalled in the two-week period and could have discussed this resolution or some other such resolution. And, instead of doing that, the government said that it did not need to discuss this with Parliament, it would simply leave it until September 24 when Parliament is back.
This was one other piece in the whole string of contemptuous actions to Parliament, contempt bred out of disrespect for the House on the one hand but fear on the other, fear that it does not know how to control the House, fear that it cannot control what the opposition says in this House, fear that it is going to have its sins exposed by the Opposition in this House.
I do not mean necessarily bad things but I mean the unsatisfactory parts of its policies are exposed and brought to light in this Chamber. That is what this place is all about, so that the deficiencies in the government's performance can be brought to light so that it can correct them, but the government resents having them exposed. I do not know why. It should say it is sorry it made a mistake and will fix it at once. But you never hear that, Mr. Speaker.
Who has been here in Question Period and has heard a minister of the Crown rise in his place and say, "The hon. member has a good point. There is a problem there. We will have to do something about that and I will see that it is corrected", and report to the hon. member the next day. It does not happen, the government never admits there was something wrong. If a minister of the Crown does not want to answer the question he always says how bad things were under the previous Liberal regime and how much better they are today. What nonsense that is. What Canadian alive today thinks things were worse under the previous Liberal regime, other than the members of the Cabinet who sit opposite. Virtually every Canadian you speak to says we have never, ever, ever, had such a bad government as this one.
No wonder it is afraid to face the people's representatives in Parliament. No wonder it sent the troops abroad and when there was a hue and ciy it said, "Well, we are not calling Parliament. The last thing we need is a place for those people to utter their hues and cries and object to this".

Well, we do not object to it as long as these troops are under the purview, under the control of the United Nations. We support this; and we have said that all along. And we have said it because this effort on the part of the United Nations represents, as my hon. friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception has said, the first time the international community has acted in concert to deal with a world crisis. We have participating in this United Nations force, representatives of Third World countries, of middle powers and of the great powers and it is supported by all the great powers. Never before in the history of the United Nations has there been this kind of support for this kind of initiative. I think Canada, as a staunch supporter of the United Nations and its work, is delighted and should be delighted to be involved in it.
But surely we should have been consulted about our involvement. Surely that is reasonable and fair. Surely the people who have elected their representatives to sit here ought to have consultation, they ought to have some input into it and some discussion about it before it happens. And that is what I am objecting to, that that was denied.
We also feel that the attempt of the amendment that we have moved to this resolution, tries to assert in stronger terms the importance of the United Nations role in the entire crisis and the fact that we believe the Canadian troops should be under the direct control of the United Nations. We supported and continue to support the resolution that the government sought to introduce on October 16 in this House. And we would have preferred that that resolution be before us for debate now, because we believe that that resolution more accurately states what is intended by the resolution and the two amendments which are before us. We support that motion and still support that motion. And if we could have a vote on that one, we would support it.
I know that the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway is going to tell us that his party supports it too. At least, I think it does; it did the other day, but it may change. New Democratic Party policy, as I heard earlier, changes from day to day. Earlier this year the hon. member for Kamloops was up, speaking about the Senate. The NDP have been around the place, up the tree, and down the hole on the Senate so often that I do not know whether the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway could tell us the party position on the Senate. He must be even more
confused than the hon. member for Kamloops who is completely baffled. I remember asking him a question last summer about their views on the Senate. He gave me an answer which was at variance with what he said a week before. Then he told me that that was a re-interpretation of a resolution passed at some convention they had had a few weeks before that. And that was different from the policy of the previous convention, because they no longer wanted to abolish it and they were in the process of forming some new policy on the Senate which I thought he did announce the night before, but apparently he had not. It was something different.
Really the confusion and obfuscation on the part of that party and its policies is sometimes a little disconcerting. I wish the hon. member for Kamloops were here, because I would be delighted to hear his views on this particular set of motions. I believe he was supporting the one that was to be introduced on Tuesday. I think he was aware of the terms, but I would not want to put words in his mouth.
I would be delighted to have the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway support the resolutions that we are supporting. We are delighted to be able to support his amendment. I think it is a reasonable and sensible one. I am sure he supports the very sensible amendment we have moved to the motion as well, and I expect he is going to vote for it when the time comes.
How?

All of the members in this party, it seems to me, have indicated with clarity our views of the position of the government on this matter, our abhorrence at its continuing contempt for Parliament, and our desire to get on with this now and allow the question to be put, and the matter to be dealt with so that the expressions of the wishes of the people of Canada can be made manifest in the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the hon. member who just spoke about the clarity of the Liberal position will want to demonstrate that in responding to the question that I want to put to him about the intentions of his party, particularly his own intentions, on the vote on this important issue.
We heard from the member for Saint-Denis. He was very clear. He intends to support the subamendment. He intends to support the amendment, and he will vote against the main motion, if, indeed, those are defeated.
We have not yet heard from the very distinguished member for Kingston and the Islands on this question. He told us that he supports a motion which is not even before the House, but he still has not told us whether he supports the government motion which in fact is before the House. Now, I know his colleagues have dodged, bobbed, weaved and tried to avoid this question with one noble exception, Mr. Speaker, but I want to give the member for Kingston and the Islands-

Mr. Speaker, I know that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is somewhat rattled these days by the fact that he has a New Democrat right in the heart of his federal constituency, elected from the provincial constituency of Kingston. I know that rattles him.
I know that he is as confused as I am by the goings on of his Liberal colleagues in the Senate. But I want to ask the member this very straightforward question: Does the
Government Orders
member in fact support the motion of the government which is on the Order Paper and which will be voted upon at six o'clock on Tuesday evening, or is he going to wait and refuse to tell the people of Canada and his constituents? Perhaps he has not made up his mind yet, that is entirely possible. How is he going to vote, yes or no, on the government motion?

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the same mischief that the hon. member has been trying to put out all evening, but I am delighted to answer his question.
First, I must say I expect that the amendment that we moved will carry, so I think his question is entirely hypothetical. I fully expect that the members on the other side of the House will see the wisdom of our amendment, the folly of their ways, and vote for the amendment and I expect it will carry.
I can tell the hon. member without any shadow of a doubt, without any possible doubt, that I would vote for the amended resolution. That should make things crystal clear in his mind. I hope he understands that.
My expectation is the amendment to the amendment will carry, the amendment will then carry, and then we will vote for the amended motion which will then carry. I hope that that clarifies things for the hon. member.
He has raised a hypothetical question. He raises the question of what am I going to do if the amendment to the amendment is defeated, the amendment is defeated, and we are left to vote on the main motion. I will tell the hon. member my expectation is that I will vote against the main motion. But something could happen between now and Tuesday at six o'clock that would persuade me to change my mind. If that happens, then I might rise on Tuesday at six o'clock and vote the other way.
I invite the hon. member to attend in the House on Tuesday night at six o'clock and watch. He will see me vote. God willing, I will be here and I intend to vote the way I have indicated unless something changes.
Having said that, I know that the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway is planning a foray into Kingston and the Islands this weekend. I can only say how delighted I am to welcome him to my riding and I hope that he will be the very model of decorum and good behaviour and say all the right things to my constituents when he is visiting in the delightful riding of Kingston and the Islands.
